<reason>Side A built a stronger path to victory by exposing a fatal contradiction in B's position: claiming users are "reflexively skeptical" of sponsored content while simultaneously arguing that explicit disclosure "breaks authenticity." A's pressure questions forced B to concede that general skepticism does not identify specific paid products—undermining B's claim that current standards are sufficient. A effectively demonstrated that broadcast-grade disclosure (one-second verbal plus visual banner) is feasible in social formats without requiring scheduled breaks, using the morning-show host example to dismantle B's "square peg" argument. While B offered a sophisticated "parity of form versus protection" distinction, it failed to overcome the concession that the "perceived unmediated relationship" depends on obscuring commercial contracts—a mechanism A convincingly framed as consumer deception. A's closing crystallized this clash effectively, whereas B remained defensive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 (Turn 7), where A answered B's technical pressure questions with concrete broadcast analogies (chyrons, traffic sponsorships) and then weaponized B's own concession about authenticity—that naming the sponsorship destroys the video's value—to prove that value depends on deception.</best_rebuttal>
